---

**What "15 February 1750/1" means**

This is a **double-dated year** — a notation used by careful English clerks before the Calendar Act of 1752. In England at that time, the legal year began on **25 March (Lady Day)**, not 1 January. - **1750** by the old English civil reckoning
- **1751** by the modern (and Continental) reckoning

To prevent confusion, clerks wrote both years with a slash: **1750/1**.

---

> 15 February 1750/1 (O.S.) = **15 February 1751** (N.S.)

**What "1750/1" normally means**

In English records before 1752, the civil year began on 25 March (Lady Day), not 1 January. So dates falling between 1 January and 24 March carried two year numbers: the Old Style year still in force by the English civil reckoning, and the New Style year already in force by modern (1 January) reckoning. A scribe writing "6 February 1750/1" was saying: *this is February of what I call 1750, but what you will call 1751.*

**Why 25 March is different**

25 March is Lady Day itself — the day the Old Style year increments. On that day both years agree. There is no gap to bridge, so a slash there is anomalous: the two year counts are the same from 25 March onward in Old Style England. The slash should not be there.

**What to do**

Do not mechanically resolve "1750/1" to 1751 for this date. Instead:

1. **Check the surrounding register entries.** Look at the few entries immediately before and after this marriage to see where the scribe's year turns over. That will tell you whether this was still being treated as 1750 or already as 1751.
2. **Check whether the slash might be a scribal slip** — clerks sometimes wrote double-date notation out of habit even when it did not apply.
3. **Record it in your notes exactly as written:** **25 March 1750/1**, with a flag noting the anomaly and the uncertainty about which year the clerk intended.

**In your research notes**, hold it as **25 March 1750/1 (anomalous double date; see register context)** until the surrounding entries clarify the clerk's intent.

---

In short: a double date on 25 March itself is unusual because Lady Day is the exact day the year turns — both Old Style and New Style agree on that day. Before committing to either 1750 or 1751, consult the entries around this record in the register to see how the clerk was counting years at that point.
